newsitem.title: TURKEY: Israel's Levy seeks improved ties to Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Levy seeks improved ties to Turkey.

text.p: Israel's Foreign Minister David Levy, starting a visit to Turkey, said on Tuesday that a majority in the overwhelmingly Moslem country supported expanded ties with the Jewish state.

But the success of his two-day mission hinged in part on his ability to convince Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan that political progress should keep pace with increasing military cooperation between the two regional powers.
"Growing relations between the two countries are supported by the majority of (our) two countries," Levy said at Ankara airport before heading for a series of high-level talks.

"The ratification of the free trade agreement between Turkey and Israel is proof of that," he said before heading for a series of high-level consultations. Turkish MPs backed the trade measures late last week, with support from the ruling Islamists.
Levy's visit included a meeting later on Tuesday with Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader and a longstanding critic of Israel.
Their talks had been very much in doubt as late as Monday afternoon, when Erbakan finally agreed to see the Israeli envoy.

Erbakan's reticence, rooted in domestic politics and ideological affinities with Israel's Arab rivals, provoked an angry outburst from the Israeli embassy in Ankara, frustrated by the prime minister's late reply.
Nonetheless, Levy made clear he hoped to smooth relations with Erbakan and his Islam-based Welfare Party in a bid for political ties more in line with warm military and commerical links.
Erbakan won a slim plurality in general elections in 1995 after campaigning to renounce a military training pact and other accords with Israel.
Under the deals, Israeli jets train over the Anatolian heartland, minutes from Israel's longtime rival Syria. Israel is also upgrading Turkey's ageing F-4 jets.
The agreements angered much of the Moslem world and some Islamists in Turkey but they remain in effect despite Welfare's public opposition. And Turkey's secularist generals insist they remain.
At the same time, commercial relations have grown steadily.

Turkey is already Israel's largest Middle East trading partner, with 1996 turnover estimated by the Israelis at $450 million. That figure could quadruple by the year 2000, they say, under the new free trade pact.
Levy hopes to cement that projected growth in talks with Turkish officials on investments and joint ventures, particularly in the fields of high-tech agriculture and construction.
He will also meet Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller of the coalition's secularist wing and President Suleyman Demirel. On Wednesday the foreign minister meets Jewish leaders in Istanbul.
